tagline.text: A pine-forest heritage campus in Baguio, opened in 1908 as a teachers' retreat

location.label: Location
location.text: Leonard Wood Road area, Baguio City

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), then overland to Baguio

children.text: Teachers' Camp opened in April 1908 as a training and vacation site for teachers, and it remains one of Baguio's oldest campuses. Early-1900s halls and lodgings still stand among the pines, and you can walk past a national heritage marker and a flower garden.

Teachers' Camp is a training complex under the Department of Education (DepEd), set on a hillside off Leonard Wood Road in Baguio. The site was established by an ordinance of Benguet Governor William Pack in December 1907. In January 1908, W. Morgan Schuster of the Bureau of Public Instruction outlined the plan, and the camp opened on April 6, 1908 as a place for teachers' training and vacation. According to Wikipedia, the first Teachers Vacation Assembly ran until May 30 of that year.

The first building went up in 1911, followed by assembly halls, dormitories, bungalow-style cottages, and dining halls. Buildings such as Benitez Hall, Ladies Hall, Teacher's Hall, Tavera Hall, and White Hall are known by name. From June 1936 to December 1941 the Philippine Military Academy (PMA) used the grounds, and General Luna Hall and others were built in that period. During the Second World War the camp served as a Japanese hospital and was badly damaged; it was repaired and reopened in 1947.

Renovations were completed for the centennial in 2008, and the camp was declared a national heritage site in May of that year. A historical marker from the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) stands on the grounds. Today the camp is used by NEAP (National Educators Academy of the Philippines), the Department of Education's teacher-training arm, and it also hosts the Police Cordillera Administrative Region Training Center (CARTC) and Philippine Sports Commission facilities, including a running track. The Pangasinan Police Academy (now CARTC) moved in in January 1971, and from 1976 to 1989 Gintong Alay track and field athletes trained here at altitude. In July 1988, Proclamation No. 290 defined the boundaries of the Teachers Camp Reservation.

As a destination, Teachers' Camp is not a flashy attraction but a place to walk slowly and sense old Baguio. Pine trees, flower beds, century-old wooden and stone buildings, and morning mist make for a quiet stroll. Because it is a working training facility, access may be limited on days with events or courses, so check the latest notice. The camp's name has also spread widely through ghost stories about its old buildings. In November 2026, GMA News reported on a horror special of the program "Kapuso Mo, Jessica Soho" and named buildings such as Roxas Hall, Quirino Hall, Escoda Hall, Abada Hall, and Guest House 10. The report stressed that these claims are unverified, and the camp superintendent, Dr. Diosdado Medina, urged visitors to appreciate the camp beyond the ghost stories, saying that improvements to the garden, museum, and lighting are under way. Some visitors come because of the rumors, but it is better to think of this as a place to see history and the forest.

A cast-iron historical marker stands beside the amphitheater, below C. M. Recto Hall. It records the camp's history, including its founding in December 1907, its first administrator M. K. Hazelton, and its first Filipino director Alberto Dalusung. The text is in Filipino.

Buildings from different eras, including Benitez Hall, Teacher's Hall, Tavera Hall, and General Luna Hall, are scattered along the hillside. Some are managed as heritage buildings, so it is best to admire their exteriors and surroundings on foot. Other named buildings include Roxas Hall, Quirino Hall, Escoda Hall, and Abada Hall, and some were used as hospitals during the war. Their present use depends on the training schedule, so ask before approaching any building.

The flower garden is what visitors praise most in their reviews. The camp management has also said it is working on garden improvements. Bloom times vary from year to year, so check locally if you want to time your visit.
Set about 1,500 m up in Baguio's highlands, the grounds are wrapped in pine forest. Mornings are misty and cool, and even a short walk takes the heat of the city off you.
The amphitheater next to the historical marker is an outdoor space used for events. When nothing is on, it is a quiet place to sit and rest, and it is easy to photograph.

blocks.title: Everyday life of a teacher-training campus

children.text: This is a living facility where NEAP courses, police training, and athletic training continue. Filipino teachers gathering here each school break to take courses is the camp's tradition of more than 100 years. The running track on the grounds is where national athletes trained at altitude in the 1970s and 1980s, and the Sports Commission still maintains the facilities.

When no training is scheduled, the dormitories and cottages are reported to be rented to tourists. A night among the pines is the camp's biggest draw, but reservations are handled separately, so confirm locally.

items.title: 1–2 hour walking route
items.subtitle: From the gate to the marker and garden

children.text: Tell the gate staff the purpose of your visit and confirm whether entry is possible. Instructions may differ depending on the training schedule.
Walk up the hillside and look at the exteriors of old buildings such as Benitez Hall and Teacher's Hall.
Read the NHCP historical marker beside the amphitheater below C. M. Recto Hall and take a photo.
Rest as you walk through the flower garden and along the pine paths.
Leave and take a taxi or jeepney to Wright Park or downtown.
The grounds are large and hilly, so wear comfortable shoes.

items.title: Half-day Baguio route
items.subtitle: From the camp to Wright Park

children.text: If you arrived on an overnight bus from Manila, leave your bags at your lodging and have breakfast.
Stroll through Teachers' Camp and see the marker.
Take the jeepney route toward Mines View to visit Wright Park and The Mansion.
Head back downtown for lunch and a rest at Session Road and Burnham Park.
The same jeepney route passes several attractions, so it is easy to combine them into one day.

items.title: Two-day overnight route
items.subtitle: A night in the pine forest

children.text: Check in at the camp lodging and show your reservation confirmation when you unpack. Ask the reservation office for the check-in time.
Walk once around the grounds before sunset and look at the buildings and the marker.
Go downtown for dinner on Session Road and see Burnham Park at night.
Early the next morning, stroll the misty pine paths and take photos at the flower garden.
Check out and head to Wright Park or Mines View Park.
It is dark and cool at night, so bring a flashlight and a jacket. Whether lodging is available depends on the training schedule.
Direct buses such as Victory Liner and Genesis run to Baguio from Manila's Caloocan, Pasay, and Cubao terminals and from PITX.
Travel time is about
5–7 hours
depending on the departure terminal and traffic, and night trips are generally said to be faster.

From the Baguio bus terminal, continue to Teachers' Camp by taxi or jeepney.
The Baguio-Plaza-Mines View jeepney route, which starts on Lower Mabini Street, passes Teachers' Camp, the Baguio Botanical Garden, and Wright Park.
Tell the driver you are getting off at Teachers' Camp. The fare is listed at around

A taxi from Session Road or Burnham Park is listed at about
and varies with traffic.
Say you are heading toward Trancoville or Mines View, and ask to be dropped at Teachers' Camp.
The entrance is off Leonard Wood Road, and parking is reported to be available on the grounds, but check the parking fee locally.
You can walk from SM City Baguio, but it is an uphill climb.
Baguio is cool all year because of its elevation, but the dry and rainy seasons differ a great deal. On rainy days, fog and wet paths can make it unpleasant to look at the buildings.
For gardens and walks, a weekday morning in the dry season is best. On days with training sessions, it may be crowded or some areas may be restricted, so check the latest notice.

rows: Cool and dry; nights can drop to around 10℃

items.label: Entrance fee
items.price: Generally free on foot (a donation of about ₱20 has been requested)
items.note: Two travel guides list free pedestrian entry, but no official fee schedule was found, so confirm locally. Booking sports facilities or dorm rooms costs extra, and drivers may pay a parking fee

items.label: Jeepney
items.note: Traditional jeepney minimum fare. Baguio and Benguet restored ₱13 in June 2026, while a nationwide adjustment on Sept 28 was reported as ₱14; the reports conflict, so confirm locally

items.label: Taxi
items.note: Short ride from Session Road; varies with traffic. The flag-down rate was reported provisionally raised from ₱50 to ₱65 in Sept 2026

items.label: Lodging (dormitory)
items.note: Two travel blogs say ₱300–500 and ₱500–800, and a 2013 post says ₱200, so they differ widely. Not official; always confirm with the reservation office

items.label: Lodging (cottage)
items.note: Depends on size and facilities; blog figures are ₱1,500–3,000 and ₱1,500–4,000. Teacher or government-employee discounts may apply

items.label: Bus from Manila
items.note: Regular air-conditioned about ₱485–660 (₱655 from Cubao in Sept 2026), first class about ₱800–1,050. May rise with fuel prices and peak season

Dormitories and cottages inside the camp are reported to be open to tourists when no training is scheduled. I could not find an official reservation notice, so ask directly about availability and rates. Near the grounds there are several transient houses (homestays) and guesthouses, and many travelers look for lodging within walking distance.

A restaurant on the grounds is not always open, so it is safer to eat downtown before you come in. Restaurants cluster around Session Road and Burnham Park. Visitor reviews say free drinking water is available, but bring your own bottle.

Outside the grounds, a jeepney or taxi gets you to the downtown dining area within minutes. Combined with a visit to the old market or a stroll through a cafe street, it makes a full day. After dark the paths on the grounds are poorly lit, so take a taxi for a late return.
This is a training institution, so confirm at the gate whether you can enter. Some areas are restricted during events.

Guides differ on opening hours, listing an opening time of 6:00 or 7:00 AM and closing at 6:00 PM (resident trainees may jog earlier), and the track oval was reported open free of charge from 3:00 PM to 10:00 PM (August 2025 report). Hours may change, so confirm locally.
The grounds are large and hilly, so wear sneakers.
Mornings and evenings are cool, so bring a light jacket.
Drone photography may require permission, so ask the management first.
People may be staying in the buildings, so respect the privacy of trainees and guests when taking photos.
Combining it with Wright Park and the Botanical Garden on the same jeepney route makes for an easy day.
This is a government training complex, so the hours and areas open to visitors change with events. Check locally before you go.
Ghost rumors have been featured on television, but nothing has been confirmed as fact. Enjoy them lightly as stories only.
Lodging rates and booking methods differ by source, and no reliable official information was found. Always ask directly.
There are many slopes and steps, so anyone with limited mobility should check the route in advance.
In the rainy season the paths are slippery and the fog is thick, so be careful.
One of Baguio's best-known parks, reached on the same jeepney route and famous for horseback riding and pond boats.
A viewpoint area with souvenir shops, near the end of the jeepney route.
A lake park in the middle of downtown where you can rent bikes and boats.
Baguio's main street, lined with restaurants and shops.
A pine-forest complex that was turned from an American colonial-era military base into a resort.
